newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Strong growth in Philippine banks despite squeeze.
newsitem.headline: Strong growth in Philippine banks despite squeeze.

text.p: The Philippine banking industry is likely to register strong earnings growth in the coming years despite a margin squeeze due to heightened competition, banking leaders and analysts said on Thursday.
At present, there are more than 50 commercial banks serving an economy which has been steadily expanding by more than 5.0 percent in the past three years.

Last year, most commercial banks posted double-digit growth in net profits with the biggest, Metropolitan Bank and Trust Co, registering a staggering 43 percent expansion to 5.003 billion ($190 million) pesos.
This year, analysts were expecting earnings in the sector to grow by an average of 20 to 25 percent.

"The strong economic growth has boosted demand for loans -- including infrastructure financing, consumer and export loans -- which bolstered the banking sector," Marco Lucena, an analyst at PrimeEast Securities, said.
In the past, each commercial bank lorded it over its own niche market with average return on equity as high as 28 percent in the early 1990s.
The return-on-equity ratio has thinned to 14 percent in 1995 following the liberalisation of the financial and banking industries as well as the entry of 10 new foreign banks into the country.
"The competition now is on all fronts -- investment banking, consumer lending, middle market financing," Bankers Association of the Philippines (BAP) president Rafael Buenaventura said.
Loan portfolios grew by 40 to 50 percent last year. As of October last year, total loans reached 1.040 trillion pesos which was about 40 to 45 percent of the gross domestic product.
"Banks are meeting their net income targets, but they're meeting them through sheer volume and not through spreads," Rico Gonzalez, an analyst at Philippine Asia Equity, said.

He said margins were getting tighter due to declining interest rates. With the two percentage point reduction in banks' reserve requirements this year, interest rates were seen likely to slide further.
Analysts said banks would now shift their focus to finding cheaper funds rather than honing their lending strategy.
Loan to deposit ratios have climbed to around 60 to 70 percent, meaning that loan demand is fast catching up on the banks' deposits' base. Deposits are the cheapest sources of funds for banks.
"There will be a pressure on the funding side ... It's becoming a game of costs for the banks," Gonzalez said.

Buenaventura said most of the banks are addressing the problem by either increasing their capital through rights issues or through mergers. He said many banks were on the lookout for merger or acquisition opportunities including his own.
Others were resorting to floating foreign currency certificates of deposits to tap cheaper foreign exchange funds.

On the lending side, a senior banker recently expressed concern about the quality of credit being extended by banks after some banks launched aggressive lending strategy, especially to the real estate sector.
Nevertheless, most analysts still see banking issues as safe bets in the equities market.

"Banks are riding on the boom of the economy. There's no other sector which has benefited more on a surging economy except the banking sector," said Rachel Evangelista, an analyst at All Asia Capital.
Conversion rate: $1 = 26.30 pesos
